stem: What is meant by **codominance**?

options.content: Both alleles in a heterozygous organism contribute to the phenotype
options.rationale: For example, a person with alleles for A and B has blood group AB.

options.content: One allele completely hides the effect of the other
options.rationale: That describes complete dominance, as in polled and horned cattle.

options.content: The heterozygote is an even blend, part-way between the two homozygotes
options.rationale: A blend (such as evenly pink flowers) is incomplete dominance; in codominance both features show.

options.content: Two different genes control the same feature
options.rationale: Codominance involves two alleles of one gene.

explanation: In codominance neither allele is dominant over the other: a heterozygote shows the effects of both alleles, such as both antigens in blood group AB or both red and white hairs in a roan cow.
hints: Think of blood group AB.

stem: How many different alleles of the ABO blood group gene are there in the human population?

options.rationale: Each person carries two alleles, but the population has more kinds.
There are four blood groups, but only three alleles.
The alleles are $\text{I}^\text{A}$, $\text{I}^\text{B}$ and $\text{I}^\text{o}$.
There are six possible genotypes, made from three alleles.

explanation: The ABO gene has three alleles: $\text{I}^\text{A}$, $\text{I}^\text{B}$ and $\text{I}^\text{o}$. They combine in pairs to give six genotypes and four blood groups.
hints: Count the alleles, not the blood groups.

stem: True or false: a person with blood group O has the genotype $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive, so group O appears only when a person has two $\text{I}^\text{o}$ alleles.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive to both $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$, so group O always has the genotype $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$.

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive, so a person can have group O only when no $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{B}$ allele is present: the genotype must be $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$.
hints: Is $\text{I}^\text{o}$ dominant or recessive?

stem: Which genotype gives blood group **AB**?

options.rationale: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so this person is group A.
$\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ are codominant, so both antigens are made.
$\text{I}^\text{B}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so this person is group B.
Two $\text{I}^\text{o}$ alleles give group O.

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ are codominant: a person with both, $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$, makes both antigen A and antigen B and has blood group AB.
hints: Which two alleles are codominant?

stem: What is the blood group of a person with the genotype $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$?

rejected.feedback: There is no group BO: $\text{I}^\text{B}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so the person is group B.
$\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive, so it does not show when $\text{I}^\text{B}$ is present: the person is group B.

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{B}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so a person with genotype $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$ has blood group B.
hints: Which allele is recessive?

stem: Which genotypes are possible for a person with blood group **A**?

options.rationale: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ is also group A.
$\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ is also group A.
$\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ is group AB, because $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ are codominant.
Both contain $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and no $\text{I}^\text{B}$.

explanation: Group A results from $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ or from $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$, because $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$. $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ is group AB.
hints: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$ but codominant with $\text{I}^\text{B}$.

stem: A man with blood group AB ($\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$) and a woman with blood group O ($\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$) have children. Complete the expected percentages of their children with each blood group.

payload.template: Group A: {{blank:a}} %. Group B: {{blank:b}} %. Group AB: {{blank:ab}} %. Group O: {{blank:o}} %.

explanation: The man's gametes carry $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{B}$; the woman's carry only $\text{I}^\text{o}$. The children are $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ (group A) or $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$ (group B), 50% each. No child can be AB (no $\text{I}^\text{B}$ with $\text{I}^\text{A}$) or O (the man has no $\text{I}^\text{o}$).
hints: List the gametes of each parent.
Can the man pass on $\text{I}^\text{o}$?

stem: Match each genotype with its blood group.

right.content: It cannot be worked out from the genotype

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ is group A; $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$ is group B because $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive; $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ is group AB because the two alleles are codominant; $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$ is group O. A genotype always fixes the blood group.
hints: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ are codominant; $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive.

stem: Two parents both have blood group A and are both heterozygous ($\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$). What is the probability that their first child will have blood group **O**? Give a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.

rejected.feedback: Both parents carry $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so they can each pass it on: the chance of $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$ is 1/4.
Each parent passes on $\text{I}^\text{o}$ with a probability of 1/2, so $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$ has a probability of 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
3/4 is the probability of group A.

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o} \times \text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ gives $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$, $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$, $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ and $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$: 3 group A : 1 group O, so the probability of group O is $\frac{1}{4}$.
hints: Draw a Punnett square with gametes $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from each parent.

stem: A woman with blood group AB has children with a man with blood group A whose genotype is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$. Which list gives **all** the blood groups their children could have?

options.rationale: $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ give A, $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ gives AB and $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$ gives B.
The woman can pass on $\text{I}^\text{B}$ and the man $\text{I}^\text{o}$, giving $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$, which is group B.
Group O needs $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from both parents, but the woman has no $\text{I}^\text{o}$ allele.
Only children who receive $\text{I}^\text{B}$ from the mother and $\text{I}^\text{A}$ from the father are AB.

explanation: Gametes: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{B}$ from the woman; $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from the man. Children: $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ (A), $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ (A), $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ (AB) and $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$ (B). Group O is impossible because the woman cannot pass on $\text{I}^\text{o}$.
hints: Write out the four combinations of gametes.

stem: A child has blood group **O**. Which blood group could **not** belong to either of the child's parents?

options.rationale: A group A parent can be $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ and pass on $\text{I}^\text{o}$.
A group B parent can be $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$ and pass on $\text{I}^\text{o}$.
An AB parent ($\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$) has no $\text{I}^\text{o}$ allele to pass on.
A group O parent ($\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$) always passes on $\text{I}^\text{o}$.

explanation: A group O child is $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$ and received $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from each parent. Parents of groups A, B or O can carry $\text{I}^\text{o}$, but a group AB parent ($\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$) cannot.
hints: What allele must each parent have passed to a group O child?

stem: In Shorthorn cattle, the alleles for red coat ($\text{C}^\text{R}$) and white coat ($\text{C}^\text{W}$) are codominant, and heterozygous cattle are roan. A roan bull is mated with white cows, and 24 calves are born. How many of the calves would you expect to be **roan**?
explanation: Roan bull $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$ × white cows $\text{C}^\text{W}\text{C}^\text{W}$ gives $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$ (roan) and $\text{C}^\text{W}\text{C}^\text{W}$ (white) in a 1 : 1 ratio, so half of the 24 calves, 12, are expected to be roan.
workedSolution:
1. Bull's gametes: $\text{C}^\text{R}$ or $\text{C}^\text{W}$; cows' gametes: all $\text{C}^\text{W}$.
2. Calves: $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$ (roan) and $\text{C}^\text{W}\text{C}^\text{W}$ (white), 1 : 1.
3. Expected roan calves $= \frac{1}{2} \times 24 = 12$.
hints: What genotype must a roan animal have?

stem: Why is the roan coat of Shorthorn cattle an example of **codominance**?

options.content: Because every hair of a roan animal is an even pinkish colour
options.rationale: Roan animals have a mixture of red hairs and white hairs, not blended hairs.

options.content: Because a heterozygous animal has both red hairs and white hairs
options.rationale: Both alleles are expressed in the phenotype.

options.content: Because the red allele is dominant to the white allele
options.rationale: If red were dominant, heterozygous cattle would be red, not roan.
Roan cattle are heterozygous; homozygous cattle are red or white.

explanation: A roan animal is heterozygous. Both alleles contribute to its phenotype: some hairs are red and some are white, growing side by side.
hints: Do both alleles show in the heterozygote?

stem: True or false: in the ABO system, the allele $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{A}$.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not quite. $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive: $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ is group A, not group O.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive to both $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$.

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{o}$ is recessive. A person with $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ has group A, because $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$.
hints: What blood group is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$?

stem: A father has blood group A and a mother has blood group B. Their first child has blood group O.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why both parents must be heterozygous.

points.description: The child (group O) is $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$, so the child received $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from each parent
The father (group A) must therefore be $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ and the mother (group B) $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$: each has one dominant allele and one $\text{I}^\text{o}$

parts.explanation: A group O child has the genotype $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$, so the child received $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from both parents. The father has group A, so he must have $\text{I}^\text{A}$ as well: he is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$. The mother has group B, so she must be $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$. Both parents are heterozygous.

options.rationale: An $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ father could not pass on $\text{I}^\text{o}$.
Group A with an $\text{I}^\text{o}$ allele to pass on.
$\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ is group AB, not A.
$\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$ is group O, not A.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What is the probability that their next child will have blood group **AB**? Give a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.

rejected.feedback: The child needs $\text{I}^\text{A}$ from the father (1/2) and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ from the mother (1/2): 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
The father can pass on $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and the mother $\text{I}^\text{B}$, so AB is possible.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which blood groups are possible for further children of this couple?

options.rationale: AB ($\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$) and O ($\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$) are also possible.
Group O is possible: the couple already have a group O child.
Each child has an equal chance of A, B, AB or O.
$\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ × $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$ gives 1 AB : 1 A : 1 B : 1 O.

explanation: The group O child is $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$, so each parent carries $\text{I}^\text{o}$: father $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$, mother $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$. Their children can be AB, A, B or O, each with probability $\frac{1}{4}$.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Child O $= \text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$: one $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from each parent.
2. (b) Father is group A and carries $\text{I}^\text{o}$: $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$. Mother: $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$.
3. (c) Gametes: father $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{o}$; mother $\text{I}^\text{B}$ or $\text{I}^\text{o}$. AB needs $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$: $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$.
4. (d) The four combinations give AB, A, B and O.
hints: Start with the child: what is the genotype of a group O person?

stem: In Shorthorn cattle, the alleles for red coat and white coat are codominant. Heterozygous cattle have a roan coat. A farmer wants a herd in which every animal is roan.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which alleles does a roan animal have?

options.content: One allele for red coat and one allele for white coat
options.rationale: Roan cattle are heterozygous.
That genotype gives a red coat.
That genotype gives a white coat.
There is no separate roan allele: roan is what the heterozygote looks like.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: The farmer mates roan bulls with roan cows. What percentage of the calves would you expect to be roan?

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the farmer cannot produce a herd that breeds true for a roan coat.

points.description: Roan cattle are heterozygous, so each passes on the red allele or the white allele in its gametes
Crossing roans always gives some red and some white calves (1 red : 2 roan : 1 white), so roan never breeds true

parts.explanation: Roan cattle are heterozygous, so half of their gametes carry the allele for red coat and half the allele for white coat. When two roans are mated, a quarter of the calves are red and a quarter white, with only half roan, so the herd can never be pure-breeding for roan.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which cross would give **only** roan calves?

options.rationale: This gives 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white.
This gives 1 red : 1 roan.
Every calf receives one red and one white allele.
All the calves would be red.

explanation: Roan cattle are $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$. Roan × roan gives 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white, so only 50% of calves are roan and roan never breeds true. Red ($\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{R}$) × white ($\text{C}^\text{W}\text{C}^\text{W}$) gives all $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$, all roan.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Roan $= \text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$ (heterozygous).
2. (b) $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W} \times \text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$ gives 1 $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{R}$ : 2 $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$ : 1 $\text{C}^\text{W}\text{C}^\text{W}$; roan $= \frac{2}{4} = 50\%$.
3. (c) Heterozygotes cannot breed true: red and white calves keep appearing.
4. (d) $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{R} \times \text{C}^\text{W}\text{C}^\text{W}$ gives only $\text{C}^\text{R}\text{C}^\text{W}$.
hints: Roan is the heterozygote.
Which parents can only give one kind of gamete each?

stem: Why can blood group A result from two different genotypes, while blood group AB results from only one?

options.content: Because group A is more common than group AB
options.rationale: How common a group is does not decide how many genotypes give it.

options.content: Because $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is recessive and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ is dominant
options.rationale: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ are codominant; neither is recessive.

options.content: Because people with group AB have three alleles of the gene
options.rationale: Everyone has only two alleles of each gene.

options.content: Because $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ both give A, but AB needs both codominant alleles, $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$
options.rationale: Dominance over $\text{I}^\text{o}$ hides it in group A.

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ are both group A. Group AB needs both codominant alleles, so its only genotype is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$.
hints: Compare how $\text{I}^\text{A}$ behaves with $\text{I}^\text{o}$ and with $\text{I}^\text{B}$.

stem: A man with genotype $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ has children with a woman with genotype $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$. What is the expected ratio of the children's blood groups?

options.rationale: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ + $\text{I}^\text{B}$ gives AB; $\text{I}^\text{A}$ + $\text{I}^\text{o}$ gives A.
The man always passes on $\text{I}^\text{A}$, so no child can be group B.

options.content: 1 group A : 1 group B : 1 group AB : 1 group O
options.rationale: That needs both parents to carry $\text{I}^\text{o}$; the man is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$.
Half of the woman's eggs carry $\text{I}^\text{o}$, giving $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ children of group A.

explanation: The man's gametes all carry $\text{I}^\text{A}$; the woman's carry $\text{I}^\text{B}$ or $\text{I}^\text{o}$. Children: $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ (AB) and $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$ (A) in equal numbers.
hints: The man can make only one kind of gamete.

stem: At a hospital, a baby with blood group **O** was labelled as the child of a mother with blood group **AB** and a father with blood group **A**. Use a genetic diagram to explain why the hospital should check its records. [5]

points.description: Mother (AB) is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$; her eggs carry $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{B}$
Father (A) is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$; his sperm carry $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or (possibly) $\text{I}^\text{o}$
A group O baby must be $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$, needing $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from both parents
The mother has no $\text{I}^\text{o}$ allele, so she cannot pass it on
Possible children are A, AB (and B if the father is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$), never O; so the baby cannot be theirs / the labels may have been mixed up

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The mother is group AB, so her genotype is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ and her eggs carry either $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{B}$. The father is group A, so he is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$, and his sperm carry $\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{o}$. A baby with group O must be $\text{I}^\text{o}\text{I}^\text{o}$, so it must have received $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from both parents. The mother has no $\text{I}^\text{o}$ allele, so she cannot pass one on. Her children can only be group A, AB or (if the father is $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$) B, never group O. The baby cannot be the child of this couple, so the hospital should check whether babies' labels were mixed up.

explanation: A group O child needs $\text{I}^\text{o}$ from both parents. An AB parent has no $\text{I}^\text{o}$, so a group O baby cannot be the child of an AB mother.
hints: What genotype must a group O baby have?
Which alleles can the AB mother pass on?

stem: Which two alleles of the ABO blood group gene are **codominant**?

options.rationale: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$.
$\text{I}^\text{B}$ is dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$.

options.content: None of them: the blood groups show complete dominance
options.rationale: Group AB shows that $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ are codominant.
A person with both makes both antigens: group AB.

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ are codominant, so $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ gives group AB. Both are dominant to $\text{I}^\text{o}$.
hints: Which blood group shows the effect of two alleles at once?

stem: In one kind of flowering plant, crossing a red-flowered plant with a white-flowered plant gives offspring whose flowers are all evenly **pink**, with no red or white patches. Why is this **not** a good example of codominance?

options.content: Because codominance happens only in animals
options.rationale: Codominance occurs in plants as well as in animals.

options.content: Because pink is caused by a third allele
options.rationale: Pink comes from the heterozygote; no new allele is involved.

options.content: Because the heterozygote shows a blend of the two colours, not both colours at once
options.rationale: In codominance both features appear, like red and white hairs in a roan cow.

options.content: Because codominance always gives a 3 : 1 ratio
options.rationale: Codominant crosses such as roan × roan give 1 : 2 : 1.

explanation: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed side by side, such as the red and white hairs of a roan animal or both antigens in group AB. An even pink colour is a blend in which neither colour shows fully; biologists call this incomplete dominance.
hints: In a roan cow, can you see both colours?

stem: Name the blood group that results from two **codominant** alleles being present together.

rejected.feedback: Group O results from two recessive $\text{I}^\text{o}$ alleles.
Group A can result from $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{A}$ or $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{o}$; the codominant pair $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ gives AB.
Group B can result from $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{B}$ or $\text{I}^\text{B}\text{I}^\text{o}$; the codominant pair $\text{I}^\text{A}\text{I}^\text{B}$ gives AB.

explanation: $\text{I}^\text{A}$ and $\text{I}^\text{B}$ are codominant, so a person with both has blood group AB.
hints: Both antigens are present.
